NEW: Saudi Arabia is preparing a new offensive against Yemen’s Houthis, potentially within weeks, aimed mainly at retaking the Bab el-Mandeb strait and restoring Red Sea shipping.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized, with Saudi air support. Riyadh is considering either a limited coastal assault or a broader multi-front offensive across Yemen.
The U.S. is providing intelligence and military advisers but is not expected to join combat directly. 
Pakistan has deployed 30,000–40,000 troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend against Houthi missile and drone attacks.
Riyadh believes peace talks cannot resume while the Houthis control Bab el-Mandeb.
Source: Reuters

events.text:
The commander of Hamas's Northern Gaza Brigade, who was killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza City earlier this week, had been responsible for holding numerous hostages in captivity, the military says.
The IDF says that "following extensive intelligence research," it can reveal that Izz al-Din al-Bik, who was killed on Tuesday, "commanded the captivity of Israeli hostages during the war."
The hostages under Bik's responsibility included Mia Schem, Hisham al-Sayed, Amit Buskila, Uriel Baruch, Corporal Nik Beizer, Sergeant Ron Sherman, Elia Toledano, Shani Louk, Michel Nisenbaum, Staff Sergeant Tamir Nimrodi, Yitzhak Gelerenter, Eitan Levy, Hanan Yablonka, Ron Benjamin, and Orion Hernandez.
Bik had been in the role since the previous Northern Gaza Brigade commander, Ahmed Ghandour, was killed by Israel on November 10, 2023, according to the military and Hamas.
Before that, he held other top roles, including chief of intelligence in the Northern Gaza Brigade and commander of the Western Jabalia Battalion.
"In these roles, he advanced and financed numerous attacks against Israeli civilians and was among the founders of Hamas’s Nukhba forces in northern Gaza," the military says.
In addition, Bik "commanded and participated in the infiltration into Israeli territory" during the October 7, 2023, onslaught, according to the IDF.

events.text:
🔯 False flag op to blame Iran? Iranian media raises questions over FlyDubai incident
A false flag FlyDubai hijacking was orchestrated by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drag US President Donald Trump into a new war against Iran, Press TV reports.
The alleged plot was discussed and finalized by Netanyahu and Emirati officials during the Israeli's latest visit to the UAE, an informed regional source told the publication. Netanyahu also reportedly held talks with officials from several other Arab countries to attribute the planned false flag operation to Iran.
Three days later, on September 30, Flydubai flight FZ1073 left Dubai International Airport for Ben Gurion Airport. Over northern Saudi Arabia, it transmitted the unlawful interference code, made a sharp descent, but then landed safely at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Airport in Tabuk.
🗣 Israeli officials said a co-pilot stabbed the plane's captain during the flight, but passengers and crew managed to restrain the attacker. The Omani co-pilot was reportedly detained by Saudi authorities. Netanyahu and his cabinet officials [described it as a foiled 9/11-style attack](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75472).
➡️ On October 1, US President Donald Trump suggested that the Omani co-pilot was linked to Iran and had allegedly been planted by the IRGC.
The source told Press TV that Netanyahu needs an escalation between the US and Iran, as his coalition may fail to secure a majority in the October elections, leaving him at risk of facing prison if he loses.
Some experts doubt that Trump would resume large-scale military actions against Iran ahead of the November midterm elections in the US. The US president said renewed bombing of Iran after the midterms was "possible."

events.text:
🇺🇸🚀 US rushes Patriots to fortify Saudi & Qatari energy hubs as Trump weighs hitting Iran again
Two additional Patriot missile batteries have been sent to the Gulf states in recent weeks, reports Axios.
One was deployed to protect a key Saudi oil facility, while the other was positioned to defend a major Qatari natural gas site, according to insiders.
The move reportedly aims to reassure both allies that their energy assets will stay protected if the US [resumes major combat operations](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75476) against Iran.
➡️ Saudi Arabia has been[ running low on interceptor missiles](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74699) and seeking urgent air defense support amid the fight against the Houthis.
The deployments serve a wider strategic purpose:
🔴 access to Saudi airspace would be essential for any large-scale US operations
🔴 the kingdom is unlikely to grant it without firm guarantees that its energy facilities are secure
When Trump weighed strikes on Iranian energy targets this summer, Saudi and Qatari leaders reportedly[ lobbied him to back off](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73009) - arguing that Iran would retaliate against their own oil and gas infrastructure. 
Those appeals purportedly helped shift the administration toward an [economic-pressure approach](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75065?single) instead.
Global Patriot stocks[ have been drained](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75168) by the Ukraine conflict and the Iran war, with the US shuttling batteries and munitions from other theaters to the Middle East.
